title: 200 core words
hook: two plain words, action and fruit, and two good readings of what the Gita asks
tomorrow: what do doing, being and going have in common?

segments.voice: Yesterday, 200 core words got small: the words that hold a sentence up, and iti closing Arjuna's 'I will not fight.' Today, two nouns, and an argument about them.

A coach says it before the big game: control what you can control, forget the scoreboard. Some players love it. Some hear an excuse to stop caring about winning. Both sides want to win; they disagree about what to carry into the game. The Gita has a line that starts the same argument, and two plain core words sit in it: karma and phala.
screen: `FORGET THE SCOREBOARD?` → `TWO WAYS TO HEAR IT.` → `KARMA AND PHALA.`

segments.voice: Here's the half line: karmany evadhikaras te ma phaleshu kadachana. Karma: action, a deed, a thing done; here karmani, in action. Phala: fruit, the result a deed brings; here phaleshu, in the fruits. Kadachana, ever, closes the half line like a door: never, not once, in the fruits. Krishna, to Arjuna: your claim is in action alone, never in its fruits. The verse goes on: don't let the fruit be your motive, and don't cling to not acting either. So, do results matter at all? Readers inside the tradition answer differently, and each side has a strong case. One reading: let go of the fruit entirely. Work done for a reward binds; work done as an offering frees. Later in the Gita, Krishna asks that whatever is done be offered to him. On this reading, caring about outcomes is the very knot the verse cuts. The other reading: the verse never says don't care how it turns out. It says the fruit isn't your claim, isn't owed to you. You still aim, still plan, still give it everything, since the same verse rules out slacking off. What you drop is the demand. Notice that neither reading says the work doesn't matter. They disagree about the fruit, not the doing, and each can point to people who lived it. Letting go of the outcome, or letting go of being owed it? The Gita doesn't settle it with a slogan. The two core words hold both.
screen: `KARMA: ACTION. PHALA: FRUIT.` · `YOUR CLAIM: ACTION, NEVER FRUIT.` · `ONE READING: LET THE FRUIT GO.` · `ANOTHER: THE FRUIT ISN'T OWED.` · then, large: `TWO WORDS HOLD BOTH.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you're working toward this week. Silently name the result you're hoping for, then the one action that's actually yours to do today. Hold the action, set the hoped-for result down beside you like a bag at your feet, and breathe. If the result keeps creeping back into your hands, set it down again.
Two hundred core words: plain ones that keep coming back. Today, karma, action, and phala, the fruit it bears: two words, set apart on purpose.
One to keep: 200 core words, and action and fruit are two different words. Rest easy.

howItsDone: Hindus often recite Gita 2.47 as a reminder to act without clinging to results; teachers in different schools explain it differently, and students learn karma and phala as two of the Gita's plainest words.

fork.setup: a friend reads Gita 2.47 as 'just don't care how it turns out.' give her the other reading's best case.

fork.reveal: the steelman: the fruit isn't your claim, but the same verse rules out slacking. what's dropped is the demand, not the effort.

original.note: Sanskrit: your claim is in action alone (Bhagavad Gita 2.47).

trapdoor: what you thought: karma means cosmic payback.
what it means: in Gita 2.47, karma is action and phala its fruit; the claim is to the first, never the second.
what a scholar hears: karmani, locative of karman; phaleshu, locative plural of phala; readers differ on whether the verse asks to drop desire for results or the sense of being owed them.

chat.meaning: Gita 2.47 gives a claim to action, never to its fruit, and rules out quitting. Some read it as letting go of results, some as dropping the demand.

karma.meaning: action, a deed, a thing done

phala.meaning: fruit: the result a deed brings

Krishna.meaning: the god who teaches Arjuna in the Gita
